question.text: Total return on long futures + cash =

answer.text: Equivalent to holding underlying physical asset

explanation.text: The Logic: Holding a long futures position fully collateralised with cash (or a cash-equivalent such as Treasury bills) replicates the economic exposure of owning the underlying physical asset. The futures position captures the price movement of the underlying, while the cash collateral earns the risk-free rate that is already embedded — by no-arbitrage — in the futures price relative to the spot. The combined return therefore mirrors the total return of the underlying, which is why long futures plus cash is described as a "synthetic" long position in the underlying. The Trap: A zero return ignores the price exposure that the futures position provides. A negative return would only arise from leverage and adverse moves, which are not the structural feature of a fully-funded position. "Random" is not a defined outcome of a synthetic long position. Note: The cited pages of the NISM-Series-XXI-B Portfolio Managers workbook (p.103-p.107, p.321-p.322) explain derivatives, futures, margining, hedging and arbitrage but do not explicitly state that long futures plus cash equals holding the physical underlying asset (synthetic equity equivalence) in the pages checked. The framing above is general derivatives / synthetic-position knowledge.
